subject: Fridge spelling
query: why does refrigerator not have a d
title: Why does refrigerator not have a d, but fridge does?
answer: Because "fridge" is a newer clipped word that follows a different spelling rule. "Refrigerator" comes from Latin "refrigerare," with no d. When people shortened it to "frij" in the early 1900s, writers added a d so it would be spelled like bridge and lodge, which is how English normally writes a "j" sound after a short vowel.
body:
"Refrigerator" has been in English since the early 1600s. It comes from "refrigerate," from the Latin verb "refrigerare," built on "frigus," meaning cold, the same root behind "frigid." In Latin the g was hard; English later softened it, but the spelling never needed a d.

The short form arrived much later, after home refrigerators spread. Merriam-Webster dates the clipped word to the 1920s, and it first appeared in print as "frig." That spelling had a problem: by ordinary rules "frig" should rhyme with "rig." Writing "frige" would not work either, since a silent e makes the vowel long, so it would look like it rhymes with "oblige."

English has a standard fix for this. After a short vowel, the "j" sound is usually spelled "dge": badge, edge, bridge, lodge, fudge. After a long vowel or a consonant it is just "ge": age, huge, change. "Fridge" simply follows that pattern. For a while British writers used "'fridge," with an apostrophe marking the missing letters, and dictionaries once labeled the word chiefly British before it became standard everywhere.

So the d is not a mistake or a leftover from "refrigerator." It is a pronunciation guide, added so the short word would be read correctly. A popular theory credits the Frigidaire brand with shaping the word; dictionaries do not confirm that, and the -dge spelling rule fully explains the d on its own.

faq.q: Is it spelled fridge or frig?
faq.a: "Fridge" is the standard spelling today. "Frig" was an early variant and is now rare.
Refrigerator. "Refridgerator" is a common misspelling influenced by "fridge."

faq.q: When did people start saying fridge?
faq.a: The short form appeared in print in the early 20th century; Merriam-Webster dates it to the 1920s.

faq.q: Does Frigidaire have anything to do with the word fridge?
faq.a: It is a popular theory, but major dictionaries trace "fridge" to "refrigerator" and explain the d with the -dge spelling rule.
